fm_variable_time.description: Integrate signed acceleration and velocity, account for initial conditions and distinguish turns from instantaneous rest.

sections.title: How do I turn a time-dependent force into velocity?
sections.label: Divide by mass and integrate
sections.intro: Along a chosen line, use a signed resultant. Since mass is constant, the signed acceleration is the force divided by mass.

blocks.html: Use \(a=\frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dt}\). Find the integration constant from a known velocity.

blocks.title: Integrate a force-dependent motion model
blocks.prompt: A particle of mass \(4\) kilograms has initial velocity \(4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Its signed resultant force at time \(t\) is \(F=20 - 12 t\) newtons. Find its signed acceleration and velocity after \(1\,\mathrm s\).
blocks.hint: Use a separate initial condition every time you integrate.
blocks.solution:
Divide the net force by mass to obtain \(a=5 - 3 t\). There is a new acceleration at each time.

Integrate and use initial velocity. This gives \(v=- \frac{3 t^{2}}{2} + 5 t + 4\).

At the stated time, signed acceleration is \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) and velocity is \(\frac{15}{2}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

blocks.html: Constant-acceleration formulae do not apply if the net force varies with time.

sections.title: Why do I need a second initial condition?
sections.label: Integrate velocity once more
sections.intro: The first integration determines velocity up to a constant. A second integration introduces a new constant for the position origin.

blocks.html: Use \(v=\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}\). Displacement is the difference between final and initial position.

blocks.title: Integrate a force-dependent motion model
blocks.prompt: At \(t=0\), a particle is at \(x=3\) metres with signed velocity \(4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). The acceleration is \(a=5 - 3 t\) in SI units. Find its signed coordinate after \(1\,\mathrm s\) and its displacement over this time.
blocks.hint: Use a separate initial condition every time you integrate.
blocks.solution:
First integrate acceleration and fit the initial velocity: \(v=- \frac{3 t^{2}}{2} + 5 t + 4\).

Integrate velocity and fit the initial coordinate: \(x=- \frac{t^{3}}{2} + \frac{5 t^{2}}{2} + 4 t + 3\).

The displacement is \(6\,\mathrm m\) and the final coordinate is \(9\,\mathrm m\).

blocks.html: The final coordinate is not always the displacement from the initial point.

sections.title: Which equation gives the first stop?
sections.label: Set velocity to zero
sections.intro: A particle can have zero acceleration while still moving. A first stop occurs at the earliest accessible zero of signed velocity.

blocks.html: Find all candidate roots on the permitted interval and check the direction before the first one.

blocks.title: Find the first stop under time-dependent acceleration
blocks.prompt: A particle has initial velocity \(6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Its signed acceleration is \(a=- 3 t\) in SI units. Find the first stopping time and its displacement by then.
blocks.hint: Set velocity, not acceleration, equal to zero. Check that there is no earlier positive root.
blocks.solution:
Integrating gives \(v=6 - \frac{3 t^{2}}{2}\). The first non-negative zero is \(2\,\mathrm s\).

The motion remains in the positive direction up to that time. The displacement is \(8\,\mathrm m\).

blocks.html: Do not solve for zero acceleration instead of zero velocity.

blocks.title: Find the first stop under time-dependent acceleration
blocks.prompt: A particle has initial velocity \(\frac{45}{2}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Its signed acceleration is \(a=- 5 t\) in SI units. Find the first stopping time and its displacement by then.
blocks.hint: Set velocity, not acceleration, equal to zero. Check that there is no earlier positive root.
blocks.solution:
Integrating gives \(v=\frac{45}{2} - \frac{5 t^{2}}{2}\). The first non-negative zero is \(3\,\mathrm s\).

The motion remains in the positive direction up to that time. The displacement is \(45\,\mathrm m\).

sections.title: How do I calculate distance when velocity changes sign?
sections.label: Split at a turning time
sections.intro: Velocity has signed area on a time graph. For total distance, divide the journey into intervals with constant velocity sign and add the lengths.

blocks.html: Displacement uses \(\int v\,\mathrm dt\). Distance uses the integral of the magnitude of velocity.

figure.alt: A velocity curve crosses the time axis at A. Areas on either side of A have different signs.
figure.caption: Displacement counts the lower region negatively. For distance travelled, count the magnitudes of both regions.

blocks.title: Distinguish signed displacement from total distance
blocks.prompt: A particle has initial velocity \(6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Its signed acceleration is \(a=- 3 t\) in SI units. The acceleration law continues until \(\frac{8}{3}\,\mathrm s\). Find the signed displacement and total distance by that instant.

retry.feedback: This is the magnitude of displacement. Include the length travelled after the turn.

blocks.hint: Split distance at the first velocity sign change. Add positive lengths for the two legs.
blocks.solution:
The velocity is \(v=6 - \frac{3 t^{2}}{2}\). Its sign changes at \(2\,\mathrm s\).

The position relative to the start is \(8\,\mathrm m\) at that turn and \(\frac{176}{27}\,\mathrm m\) at the end.

The signed displacement is \(\frac{176}{27}\,\mathrm m\). The distance adds the outward leg and the length travelled back, giving \(\frac{256}{27}\,\mathrm m\).

blocks.html: The magnitude of the overall displacement can be smaller than total distance.

sections.title: What changes when the force law switches?
sections.label: Restart with a local time
sections.intro: At an ordinary switch in finite force, position and velocity agree at the boundary. A different acceleration law applies on the second interval.

blocks.html: Start the new formula from the first stage’s ending position and velocity.

blocks.title: Carry velocity and position across a change of law
blocks.prompt: A particle starts with velocity \(\frac{2}{3}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Its acceleration is \(a=3 t\) for \(\frac{3}{2}\,\mathrm s\). It then changes to \(a=5\tau\) where \(\tau\) measures time since that change. Find velocity and displacement relative to the original start after \(1\,\mathrm s\) in the second stage.
blocks.hint: Restart the clock at the switch and carry position and velocity, rather than the old acceleration law.
blocks.solution:
Integrate the first acceleration from its own initial conditions. At the switch the velocity is \(\frac{97}{24}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and displacement \(\frac{43}{16}\,\mathrm m\).

Integrate the second acceleration with new initial velocity \(\frac{97}{24}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Integrating this velocity gives the second-stage displacement.

The velocity is \(\frac{157}{24}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and total displacement is \(\frac{121}{16}\,\mathrm m\).

blocks.html: Do not re-use the original starting speed in the second stage.

blocks.title: Carry velocity and position across a change of law
blocks.prompt: A particle starts with velocity \(\frac{4}{3}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Its acceleration is \(a=5 t\) for \(\frac{5}{2}\,\mathrm s\). It then changes to \(a=7\tau\) where \(\tau\) measures time since that change. Find velocity and displacement relative to the original start after \(2\,\mathrm s\) in the second stage.
blocks.hint: Restart the clock at the switch and carry position and velocity, rather than the old acceleration law.
blocks.solution:
Integrate the first acceleration from its own initial conditions. At the switch the velocity is \(\frac{407}{24}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and displacement \(\frac{785}{48}\,\mathrm m\).

Integrate the second acceleration with new initial velocity \(\frac{407}{24}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Integrating this velocity gives the second-stage displacement.

The velocity is \(\frac{743}{24}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and total displacement is \(\frac{2861}{48}\,\mathrm m\).

examples.title: Integrate a force-dependent motion model
examples.question: A particle of mass \(3\) kilograms has initial velocity \(3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Its signed resultant force at time \(t\) is \(F=12 - 6 t\) newtons. Find its signed acceleration and velocity after \(\frac{1}{2}\,\mathrm s\).
solution: Divide the net force by mass to obtain \(a=4 - 2 t\). There is a new acceleration at each time.
Integrate and use initial velocity. This gives \(v=- t^{2} + 4 t + 3\).
At the stated time, signed acceleration is \(3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) and velocity is \(\frac{19}{4}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

examples.title: Integrate a force-dependent motion model
examples.question: At \(t=0\), a particle is at \(x=2\) metres with signed velocity \(3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). The acceleration is \(a=4 - 2 t\) in SI units. Find its signed coordinate after \(\frac{1}{2}\,\mathrm s\) and its displacement over this time.
solution: First integrate acceleration and fit the initial velocity: \(v=- t^{2} + 4 t + 3\).
Integrate velocity and fit the initial coordinate: \(x=- \frac{t^{3}}{3} + 2 t^{2} + 3 t + 2\).
The displacement is \(\frac{47}{24}\,\mathrm m\) and the final coordinate is \(\frac{95}{24}\,\mathrm m\).

examples.title: Find the first stop under time-dependent acceleration
examples.question: A particle has initial velocity \(\frac{9}{4}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Its signed acceleration is \(a=- 2 t\) in SI units. Find the first stopping time and its displacement by then.
solution: Integrating gives \(v=\frac{9}{4} - t^{2}\). The first non-negative zero is \(\frac{3}{2}\,\mathrm s\).
The motion remains in the positive direction up to that time. The displacement is \(\frac{9}{4}\,\mathrm m\).

examples.title: Find the first stop under time-dependent acceleration
examples.question: A particle has initial velocity \(\frac{25}{2}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Its signed acceleration is \(a=- 4 t\) in SI units. Find the first stopping time and its displacement by then.
solution: Integrating gives \(v=\frac{25}{2} - 2 t^{2}\). The first non-negative zero is \(\frac{5}{2}\,\mathrm s\).
The motion remains in the positive direction up to that time. The displacement is \(\frac{125}{6}\,\mathrm m\).

examples.title: Distinguish signed displacement from total distance
examples.question: A particle has initial velocity \(\frac{9}{4}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Its signed acceleration is \(a=- 2 t\) in SI units. The acceleration law continues until \(\frac{11}{6}\,\mathrm s\). Find the signed displacement and total distance by that instant.
solution: The velocity is \(v=\frac{9}{4} - t^{2}\). Its sign changes at \(\frac{3}{2}\,\mathrm s\).
The position relative to the start is \(\frac{9}{4}\,\mathrm m\) at that turn and \(\frac{671}{324}\,\mathrm m\) at the end.
The signed displacement is \(\frac{671}{324}\,\mathrm m\). The distance adds the outward leg and the length travelled back, giving \(\frac{787}{324}\,\mathrm m\).

examples.title: Carry velocity and position across a change of law
examples.question: A particle starts with velocity \(\frac{1}{3}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Its acceleration is \(a=2 t\) for \(1\,\mathrm s\). It then changes to \(a=4\tau\) where \(\tau\) measures time since that change. Find velocity and displacement relative to the original start after \(\frac{1}{2}\,\mathrm s\) in the second stage.
solution: Integrate the first acceleration from its own initial conditions. At the switch the velocity is \(\frac{4}{3}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and displacement \(\frac{2}{3}\,\mathrm m\).
Integrate the second acceleration with new initial velocity \(\frac{4}{3}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Integrating this velocity gives the second-stage displacement.
The velocity is \(\frac{11}{6}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and total displacement is \(\frac{17}{12}\,\mathrm m\).

examples.title: Carry velocity and position across a change of law
examples.question: A particle starts with velocity \(1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Its acceleration is \(a=4 t\) for \(2\,\mathrm s\). It then changes to \(a=6\tau\) where \(\tau\) measures time since that change. Find velocity and displacement relative to the original start after \(\frac{3}{2}\,\mathrm s\) in the second stage.
solution: Integrate the first acceleration from its own initial conditions. At the switch the velocity is \(9\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and displacement \(\frac{22}{3}\,\mathrm m\).
Integrate the second acceleration with new initial velocity \(9\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Integrating this velocity gives the second-stage displacement.
The velocity is \(\frac{63}{4}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and total displacement is \(\frac{581}{24}\,\mathrm m\).

related.title: Position-dependent force and the physical velocity branch

fm_variable_position.description: Use the chain rule in one dimension and identify a physical signed velocity when squared speed is known.

sections.title: Why is acceleration also v times dv/dx?
sections.label: Choose position as independent variable
sections.intro: Velocity can be described along a monotone part of the path. The chain rule converts a time derivative into a position derivative.

blocks.html: \(a=\frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dt}=\frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dx}\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}=v\frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dx}\).

blocks.title: Choose the sign after solving for squared speed
blocks.prompt: At \(x=0\) a particle moves in the positive direction with speed \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Its acceleration is \(a=\frac{2 x}{3} + \frac{3}{2}\) in SI units. Find its signed velocity at \(x=1\) metres assuming it has not turned.

retry.feedback: The square-root sign must match the stated direction of motion.

blocks.hint: The equation gives speed squared. Use the physical branch to recover signed velocity.
blocks.solution:
With position as independent variable, \(a=v\frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dx}\). Thus \(\frac12v^2\) is an antiderivative of \(\frac{2 x}{3} + \frac{3}{2}\).

Apply the initial condition to obtain \(v^2=\frac{2 x^{2}}{3} + 3 x + 25\).

Choose the positive square root because the direction is unchanged. The signed velocity is \(\frac{\sqrt{258}}{3}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

blocks.html: Do not treat a position-dependent force as a time-dependent one.

sections.title: When do I take the negative square root?
sections.label: Read the physical branch
sections.intro: The integrated result frequently gives squared velocity. On a branch without a stop, the velocity retains its starting sign.

blocks.html: Use the negative root for motion along the negative axis.

blocks.title: Choose the sign after solving for squared speed
blocks.prompt: At \(x=0\) a particle moves in the negative direction with speed \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Its acceleration is \(a=\frac{2 x}{3} - \frac{3}{2}\) in SI units. Find its signed velocity at \(x=-1\) metres assuming it has not turned.

retry.feedback: The square-root sign must match the stated direction of motion.

blocks.hint: The equation gives speed squared. Use the physical branch to recover signed velocity.
blocks.solution:
With position as independent variable, \(a=v\frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dx}\). Thus \(\frac12v^2\) is an antiderivative of \(\frac{2 x}{3} - \frac{3}{2}\).

Apply the initial condition to obtain \(v^2=\frac{2 x^{2}}{3} - 3 x + 25\).

Choose the negative square root because the direction is unchanged. The signed velocity is \(- \frac{\sqrt{258}}{3}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

blocks.html: Speed is a magnitude. A question may instead require signed velocity.

sections.title: Where can a particle stop under a position-dependent force?
sections.label: Solve the accessible energy root
sections.intro: Once squared speed is known as a function of position, a zero may mark a turning point. The direction and initial point decide which root can be reached.

blocks.html: On the initial branch require \(v^2\ge0\) up to the candidate root.

blocks.title: Locate a first stop from force as a function of x
blocks.prompt: At \(x=0\) a particle of mass \(3\) kilograms has rightwards velocity \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). The signed resultant force is \(F=- 12 x\) newtons. Find the coordinate of its first stop.

retry.feedback: The particle begins moving to positive x, so its first stop uses that side.

blocks.hint: Solve for the first accessible zero of the squared speed.
blocks.solution:
Set \(mv\frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dx}=F(x)\) and integrate in x, rather than assuming constant acceleration.

The initial condition gives \(v^2=25 - 4 x^{2}\). The positive coordinate where this vanishes is \(\frac{5}{2}\,\mathrm m\).

blocks.html: A second root on the other side of the starting point is not a first stop.

blocks.title: Locate a first stop from force as a function of x
blocks.prompt: At \(x=0\) a particle of mass \(5\) kilograms has rightwards velocity \(\frac{7 \sqrt{6}}{2}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). The signed resultant force is \(F=- 30 x\) newtons. Find the coordinate of its first stop.

retry.feedback: The particle begins moving to positive x, so its first stop uses that side.

blocks.hint: Solve for the first accessible zero of the squared speed.
blocks.solution:
Set \(mv\frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dx}=F(x)\) and integrate in x, rather than assuming constant acceleration.

The initial condition gives \(v^2=\frac{147}{2} - 6 x^{2}\). The positive coordinate where this vanishes is \(\frac{7}{2}\,\mathrm m\).

sections.title: How can velocity-squared resistance simplify in space?
sections.label: Separate the spatial equation
sections.intro: On a strictly forward branch, divide the velocity-squared force law by the positive velocity when using the chain rule.

blocks.html: With \(a=-kv^2\), the spatial equation is \(\frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dx}=-kv\) for \(v>0\).

blocks.title: Separate with position as the independent variable
blocks.prompt: A particle has positive velocity \(8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) at \(x=0\). Its acceleration while moving forwards is \(a=- v^{2}\). The speed becomes \(\frac{8}{3}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) at distance \(C\ln 3\) metres. Find the exact coefficient \(C\).
blocks.hint: Convert the differential equation to dv/dx before separating the variables.
blocks.solution:
Use \(a=v\frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dx}\) and cancel \(v\) on its positive branch.

Integrating gives \(v=8 e^{- x}\). At the target speed, \(\mathrm e^{-1x}=\frac{1}{3}\).

Therefore the distance is \(\log{\left(3 \right)}\,\mathrm m\), with coefficient \(1\).

blocks.html: Division by velocity would remove a zero-velocity branch.

sections.title: Can zero speed be a purely limiting state?
sections.label: Check the time to reach the boundary
sections.intro: A zero of squared velocity at a spatial coordinate need not occur in finite time.

blocks.html: Use the signed relation between velocity and position to test the approach.

figure.alt: A forward velocity falls linearly with position towards zero at x = L.
figure.caption: A spatial graph can show a zero speed at a position that is only approached. Solve the time equation before saying that the particle stops there.

blocks.title: Keep the physically valid branch up to a boundary
blocks.prompt: A particle starts from \(x=0\) with velocity \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Its acceleration is \(a=x - 5\). Find the velocity at \(x=\frac{10}{3}\) metres and the limiting coordinate.
blocks.hint: On a position-dependent model, a zero squared speed need not occur at a finite time.
blocks.solution:
Integrating with position gives \(v^2=x^{2} - 10 x + 25\). For \(0\le x<5\), choose \(v=5 - x\).

At the requested coordinate the velocity is \(\frac{5}{3}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). The limiting coordinate is \(5\,\mathrm m\), approached as speed tends to zero.

blocks.html: Do not call a limiting position a finite turning event without checking time.

blocks.title: Keep the physically valid branch up to a boundary
blocks.prompt: A particle starts from \(x=0\) with velocity \(\frac{35}{3}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Its acceleration is \(a=\frac{25 x}{9} - \frac{175}{9}\). Find the velocity at \(x=\frac{14}{3}\) metres and the limiting coordinate.
blocks.hint: On a position-dependent model, a zero squared speed need not occur at a finite time.
blocks.solution:
Integrating with position gives \(v^2=\frac{25 x^{2}}{9} - \frac{350 x}{9} + \frac{1225}{9}\). For \(0\le x<7\), choose \(v=\frac{35}{3} - \frac{5 x}{3}\).

At the requested coordinate the velocity is \(\frac{35}{9}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). The limiting coordinate is \(7\,\mathrm m\), approached as speed tends to zero.

examples.title: Choose the sign after solving for squared speed
examples.question: At \(x=0\) a particle moves in the positive direction with speed \(4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Its acceleration is \(a=\frac{x}{3} + 1\) in SI units. Find its signed velocity at \(x=\frac{1}{2}\) metres assuming it has not turned.
solution: With position as independent variable, \(a=v\frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dx}\). Thus \(\frac12v^2\) is an antiderivative of \(\frac{x}{3} + 1\).
Apply the initial condition to obtain \(v^2=\frac{x^{2}}{3} + 2 x + 16\).
Choose the positive square root because the direction is unchanged. The signed velocity is \(\frac{\sqrt{615}}{6}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

solution: With position as independent variable, \(a=v\frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dx}\). Thus \(\frac12v^2\) is an antiderivative of \(\frac{x}{3} - 1\).
Apply the initial condition to obtain \(v^2=\frac{x^{2}}{3} - 2 x + 16\).
Choose the negative square root because the direction is unchanged. The signed velocity is \(- \frac{\sqrt{615}}{6}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

examples.title: Locate a first stop from force as a function of x
examples.question: At \(x=0\) a particle of mass \(2\) kilograms has rightwards velocity \(2 \sqrt{3}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). The signed resultant force is \(F=- 6 x\) newtons. Find the coordinate of its first stop.
solution: Set \(mv\frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dx}=F(x)\) and integrate in x, rather than assuming constant acceleration.
The initial condition gives \(v^2=12 - 3 x^{2}\). The positive coordinate where this vanishes is \(2\,\mathrm m\).

examples.title: Locate a first stop from force as a function of x
examples.question: At \(x=0\) a particle of mass \(4\) kilograms has rightwards velocity \(3 \sqrt{5}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). The signed resultant force is \(F=- 20 x\) newtons. Find the coordinate of its first stop.
solution: Set \(mv\frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dx}=F(x)\) and integrate in x, rather than assuming constant acceleration.
The initial condition gives \(v^2=45 - 5 x^{2}\). The positive coordinate where this vanishes is \(3\,\mathrm m\).

examples.title: Separate with position as the independent variable
examples.question: A particle has positive velocity \(7\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) at \(x=0\). Its acceleration while moving forwards is \(a=- \frac{2 v^{2}}{3}\). The speed becomes \(\frac{7}{2}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) at distance \(C\ln 2\) metres. Find the exact coefficient \(C\).
solution: Use \(a=v\frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dx}\) and cancel \(v\) on its positive branch.
Integrating gives \(v=7 e^{- \frac{2 x}{3}}\). At the target speed, \(\mathrm e^{-\frac{2}{3}x}=\frac{1}{2}\).
Therefore the distance is \(\frac{3 \log{\left(2 \right)}}{2}\,\mathrm m\), with coefficient \(\frac{3}{2}\).

examples.title: Keep the physically valid branch up to a boundary
examples.question: A particle starts from \(x=0\) with velocity \(\frac{8}{3}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Its acceleration is \(a=\frac{4 x}{9} - \frac{16}{9}\). Find the velocity at \(x=\frac{8}{3}\) metres and the limiting coordinate.
solution: Integrating with position gives \(v^2=\frac{4 x^{2}}{9} - \frac{32 x}{9} + \frac{64}{9}\). For \(0\le x<4\), choose \(v=\frac{8}{3} - \frac{2 x}{3}\).
At the requested coordinate the velocity is \(\frac{8}{9}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). The limiting coordinate is \(4\,\mathrm m\), approached as speed tends to zero.

examples.title: Keep the physically valid branch up to a boundary
examples.question: A particle starts from \(x=0\) with velocity \(8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Its acceleration is \(a=\frac{16 x}{9} - \frac{32}{3}\). Find the velocity at \(x=4\) metres and the limiting coordinate.
solution: Integrating with position gives \(v^2=\frac{16 x^{2}}{9} - \frac{64 x}{3} + 64\). For \(0\le x<6\), choose \(v=8 - \frac{4 x}{3}\).
At the requested coordinate the velocity is \(\frac{8}{3}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). The limiting coordinate is \(6\,\mathrm m\), approached as speed tends to zero.

extraPractice.title: Choose the sign after solving for squared speed
extraPractice.prompt: At \(x=0\) a particle moves in the positive direction with speed \(6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Its acceleration is \(a=x + 2\) in SI units. Find its signed velocity at \(x=\frac{3}{2}\) metres assuming it has not turned.

retry.feedback: The square-root sign must match the stated direction of motion.

extraPractice.hint: The equation gives speed squared. Use the physical branch to recover signed velocity.
extraPractice.solution:
With position as independent variable, \(a=v\frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dx}\). Thus \(\frac12v^2\) is an antiderivative of \(x + 2\).

Apply the initial condition to obtain \(v^2=x^{2} + 4 x + 36\).

Choose the positive square root because the direction is unchanged. The signed velocity is \(\frac{\sqrt{177}}{2}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

extraPractice.title: Choose the sign after solving for squared speed
extraPractice.prompt: At \(x=0\) a particle moves in the negative direction with speed \(6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Its acceleration is \(a=x - 2\) in SI units. Find its signed velocity at \(x=- \frac{3}{2}\) metres assuming it has not turned.

retry.feedback: The square-root sign must match the stated direction of motion.

extraPractice.hint: The equation gives speed squared. Use the physical branch to recover signed velocity.
extraPractice.solution:
With position as independent variable, \(a=v\frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dx}\). Thus \(\frac12v^2\) is an antiderivative of \(x - 2\).

Apply the initial condition to obtain \(v^2=x^{2} - 4 x + 36\).

Choose the negative square root because the direction is unchanged. The signed velocity is \(- \frac{\sqrt{177}}{2}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

extraPractice.title: Locate a first stop from force as a function of x
extraPractice.prompt: At \(x=0\) a particle of mass \(6\) kilograms has rightwards velocity \(4 \sqrt{7}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). The signed resultant force is \(F=- 42 x\) newtons. Find the coordinate of its first stop.

retry.feedback: The particle begins moving to positive x, so its first stop uses that side.

extraPractice.hint: Solve for the first accessible zero of the squared speed.
extraPractice.solution:
Set \(mv\frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dx}=F(x)\) and integrate in x, rather than assuming constant acceleration.

The initial condition gives \(v^2=112 - 7 x^{2}\). The positive coordinate where this vanishes is \(4\,\mathrm m\).

extraPractice.title: Separate with position as the independent variable
extraPractice.prompt: A particle has positive velocity \(9\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) at \(x=0\). Its acceleration while moving forwards is \(a=- \frac{4 v^{2}}{3}\). The speed becomes \(\frac{9}{4}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) at distance \(C\ln 4\) metres. Find the exact coefficient \(C\).
extraPractice.hint: Convert the differential equation to dv/dx before separating the variables.
extraPractice.solution:
Use \(a=v\frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dx}\) and cancel \(v\) on its positive branch.

Integrating gives \(v=9 e^{- \frac{4 x}{3}}\). At the target speed, \(\mathrm e^{-\frac{4}{3}x}=\frac{1}{4}\).

Therefore the distance is \(\frac{3 \log{\left(4 \right)}}{4}\,\mathrm m\), with coefficient \(\frac{3}{4}\).

extraPractice.title: Keep the physically valid branch up to a boundary
extraPractice.prompt: A particle starts from \(x=0\) with velocity \(16\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Its acceleration is \(a=4 x - 32\). Find the velocity at \(x=\frac{16}{3}\) metres and the limiting coordinate.
extraPractice.hint: On a position-dependent model, a zero squared speed need not occur at a finite time.
extraPractice.solution:
Integrating with position gives \(v^2=4 x^{2} - 64 x + 256\). For \(0\le x<8\), choose \(v=16 - 2 x\).

At the requested coordinate the velocity is \(\frac{16}{3}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). The limiting coordinate is \(8\,\mathrm m\), approached as speed tends to zero.

sections.title: How does the net force change as speed increases?
sections.label: Find the balance speed
sections.intro: A constant forward drive and a forward-speed-dependent resistance produce a variable resultant.

blocks.html: For linear resistance in forward motion, use \(m\frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dt}=D-kv\).

figure.alt: A speed curve increases towards a horizontal dashed terminal-speed line.
figure.caption: In this model the driving force initially exceeds resistance. Their difference tends to zero as speed approaches the terminal value.

blocks.title: Find the terminal speed and one finite-time speed
blocks.prompt: A particle of mass \(4\) kilograms has initial forward speed \(4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). A constant driving force of \(40\,\mathrm N\) acts forwards and resistance magnitude is \(4\) times forward speed. Find its terminal speed and its speed at time \(\log{\left(3 \right)}\,\mathrm s\).
blocks.hint: A terminal speed is the zero of the force, not necessarily an attained finite-time speed.
blocks.solution:
The force equation is \(\frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dt}=10 - v\). Separate on the branch set by the initial speed.

Fitting the initial condition gives \(v=10 - 6 e^{- t}\). The exponential tends to zero.

The terminal speed is \(10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). At the stated time the exponential equals \(\frac{1}{3}\), giving speed \(8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

blocks.html: At terminal speed the net force is zero. That does not imply finite-time attainment.

sections.title: How does gravity compete with drag during a fall?
sections.label: Choose down as positive
sections.intro: As the particle falls faster, the drag opposing the weight increases.

blocks.html: Taking down as positive gives \(m\frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dt}=mg-kv\) with a linear resistance model.

blocks.title: Find the terminal speed and one finite-time speed
blocks.prompt: A particle falls downwards from rest under gravity \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Its upward drag force has magnitude \(4\) times its speed, and its mass is \(4\) kilograms. Find its terminal speed and its speed at time \(\log{\left(3 \right)}\,\mathrm s\).
blocks.hint: A terminal speed is the zero of the force, not necessarily an attained finite-time speed.
blocks.solution:
The force equation is \(\frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dt}=10 - v\). Separate on the branch set by the initial speed.

Fitting the initial condition gives \(v=10 - 10 e^{- t}\). The exponential tends to zero.

The terminal speed is \(10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). At the stated time the exponential equals \(\frac{1}{3}\), giving speed \(\frac{20}{3}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

blocks.html: If you choose down as positive, weight is positive and drag is negative.

sections.title: How do I find the apex with drag present?
sections.label: Solve the ascending branch
sections.intro: During ascent, both gravity and resistance are down. Use the ascending velocity sign when writing the resultant.

blocks.html: Solve the velocity equation and find its first zero. The model after that time must have appropriate force directions.

blocks.title: Find the first stop while rising against linear drag
blocks.prompt: A particle is launched straight upwards at \(\frac{40}{3}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Acceleration during the ascent is \(a=- \frac{3 v}{2} - 10\), using upwards-positive signed velocity. Its first stopping time is \(C\ln 3\) seconds. Find the exact coefficient \(C\).
blocks.hint: Use the signed acceleration only on the branch with the correct drag direction if the model is stated for ascent.
blocks.solution:
Separate \(\frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dt}=-10-kv\), with the above initial speed.

The resulting velocity is \(v=- \frac{20}{3} + 20 e^{- \frac{3 t}{2}}\). At the first stop set this to zero.

This gives stopping time \(\frac{2 \log{\left(3 \right)}}{3}\,\mathrm s\), with coefficient \(\frac{2}{3}\).

blocks.html: Do not let a model defined only for ascent automatically describe descent.

blocks.title: Find the first stop while rising against linear drag
blocks.prompt: A particle is launched straight upwards at \(16\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Acceleration during the ascent is \(a=- \frac{5 v}{2} - 10\), using upwards-positive signed velocity. Its first stopping time is \(C\ln 5\) seconds. Find the exact coefficient \(C\).
blocks.hint: Use the signed acceleration only on the branch with the correct drag direction if the model is stated for ascent.
blocks.solution:
Separate \(\frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dt}=-10-kv\), with the above initial speed.

The resulting velocity is \(v=-4 + 20 e^{- \frac{5 t}{2}}\). At the first stop set this to zero.

This gives stopping time \(\frac{2 \log{\left(5 \right)}}{5}\,\mathrm s\), with coefficient \(\frac{2}{5}\).

sections.title: Does the drag force keep the same sign after reversal?
sections.label: Restart at the apex
sections.intro: In a signed linear law, the drag term changes direction automatically as signed velocity changes sign.

blocks.html: With upwards-positive velocity, \(a=-g-kv\) represents drag opposing both positive and negative velocity.

blocks.title: Restart the velocity after the first stop
blocks.prompt: A mass moves vertically with upwards-positive acceleration \(a=- \frac{3 v}{2} - 10\). It reaches an apex and then descends. Find its downward speed \(\frac{2 \log{\left(4 \right)}}{3}\,\mathrm s\) after the apex and its limiting downward speed.
blocks.hint: Use a local time from the apex. The signed drag law reverses the drag force when velocity reverses.
blocks.solution:
Take the apex as a new zero of time. Its initial signed velocity is zero, and the force law is still valid for negative velocity.

The signed velocity after the apex is \(v=- \frac{20}{3} + \frac{20 e^{- \frac{3 t}{2}}}{3}\). Thus the downward speed at the stated time is \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

As time increases without bound the downward speed tends to \(\frac{20}{3}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

blocks.html: A fixed downwards drag arrow would incorrectly assist downward movement after the turn.

sections.title: Does a squared resistance law require a logarithm in time?
sections.label: Integrate the inverse square
sections.intro: For purely quadratic resistance on a forward branch, separate by dividing by the square of the speed.

blocks.html: \(\frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dt}=-kv^2\) gives a reciprocal expression, because \(\int v^{-2}\,\mathrm dv=-v^{-1}\).

blocks.title: Separate a quadratic resistance law
blocks.prompt: A particle of initial speed \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) moves forwards under quadratic resistance only, with signed acceleration \(a=- \frac{3 v^{2}}{4}\). Find its speed after \(\frac{2}{3}\,\mathrm s\).
blocks.hint: Integrate v to the power minus two, not v to the power minus one.
blocks.solution:
Separate using \(\frac{\mathrm dv}{v^2}=-k\,\mathrm dt\). On the positive branch, integration gives \(\frac1v=kt+\frac1u\).

Substitute the stated time. The speed is \(\frac{10}{7}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

blocks.html: If extending a quadratic drag law across a reversal, its signed force is proportional to the negative of v times its magnitude.

blocks.title: Separate a quadratic resistance law
blocks.prompt: A particle of initial speed \(7\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) moves forwards under quadratic resistance only, with signed acceleration \(a=- \frac{5 v^{2}}{4}\). Find its speed after \(\frac{4}{3}\,\mathrm s\).
blocks.hint: Integrate v to the power minus two, not v to the power minus one.
blocks.solution:
Separate using \(\frac{\mathrm dv}{v^2}=-k\,\mathrm dt\). On the positive branch, integration gives \(\frac1v=kt+\frac1u\).

Substitute the stated time. The speed is \(\frac{21}{38}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

examples.title: Find the terminal speed and one finite-time speed

examples.title: Find the first stop while rising against linear drag
examples.question: A particle is launched straight upwards at \(10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Acceleration during the ascent is \(a=- v - 10\), using upwards-positive signed velocity. Its first stopping time is \(C\ln 2\) seconds. Find the exact coefficient \(C\).

examples.title: Find the first stop while rising against linear drag

examples.title: Restart the velocity after the first stop

examples.title: Separate a quadratic resistance law

Substitute the stated time. The speed is \(\frac{6}{7}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

fm_variable_limits.description: Distinguish exact stopping events from limits and choose time or position to solve constant-power motion.

sections.title: How do I tell whether a boundary is reached in finite time?
sections.label: Solve the time model
sections.intro: An exponential can remain positive for every finite time. Zero speed or a position at a boundary can then be a limit rather than an event.

blocks.html: Evaluate both the long-time limit and whether a finite time satisfies the endpoint equation.

figure.alt: A position curve tends to a horizontal dashed line representing a finite limiting position.
figure.caption: The position can converge even though the particle never comes to rest at a finite time.

blocks.title: Distinguish an approached boundary from a finite stop
blocks.prompt: A particle starts at the origin. In SI units the speed is \(v=5 - x\) while its position is below \(5\). Does it reach \(x=5\) in finite time? Give its limiting coordinate.
blocks.hint: Solve for position as a function of time before deciding whether the boundary is reached.
blocks.solution:
Use \(\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}=k(L-x)\) and separate. The initial condition gives \(x=5 - 5 e^{- t}\).

The exponential is positive at every finite time. Thus the limiting coordinate is \(5\,\mathrm m\) but the particle never arrives there at finite time.

blocks.html: An asymptotic limit cannot be substituted as a reached boundary time.

sections.title: Can a particle travel a finite total distance without stopping?
sections.label: Integrate before taking the limit
sections.intro: Even when speed is positive at all finite times, cumulative displacement can converge.

blocks.html: For linear drag without drive, velocity decays exponentially. Integrate it to obtain the converging displacement.

blocks.title: Find a finite limiting distance without a finite stop
blocks.prompt: A particle with initial velocity \(7\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) coasts with acceleration \(a=- v\). Find its limiting distance from its starting position and the distance at time \(\log{\left(3 \right)}\,\mathrm s\).
blocks.hint: Integrate the velocity and then take its long-time limit.
blocks.solution:
Separating gives \(v=7 e^{- t}\). The speed stays positive at all finite times.

Integrating velocity from zero gives \(x=7 - 7 e^{- t}\).

The limiting distance is \(7\,\mathrm m\). At the stated time it has travelled \(\frac{14}{3}\,\mathrm m\).

blocks.html: The limit of speed alone does not determine whether total displacement is finite.

sections.title: How do I find time under a constant-power drive?
sections.label: Pick a time-based equation
sections.intro: At positive speed, a constant-power engine produces less driving force as speed increases.

blocks.html: Use \(P=Fv\) and \(F=m\frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dt}\) for purely driven motion.

blocks.title: Use constant power to obtain squared speed in time
blocks.prompt: A particle of mass \(5\) kilograms starts with positive speed \(4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). It is driven on a smooth level track by an engine of constant power \(135\,\mathrm W\). Find the time to reach speed \(7\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

fields.label: Time to reach the target speed

blocks.hint: The driving force decreases as speed increases. The power is constant, not force.
blocks.solution:
Since \(P=Fv\), Newton's second law gives \(mv\frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dt}=P\) on the positive-speed branch.

Integrating gives \(v^2=54 t + 16\). The required time is \(\frac{11}{18}\,\mathrm s\).

blocks.html: A constant-power engine does not exert constant force.

blocks.title: Use constant power to obtain squared speed in time
blocks.prompt: A particle of mass \(7\) kilograms starts with positive speed \(6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). It is driven on a smooth level track by an engine of constant power \(225\,\mathrm W\). Find the time to reach speed \(11\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

fields.label: Time to reach the target speed

blocks.hint: The driving force decreases as speed increases. The power is constant, not force.
blocks.solution:
Since \(P=Fv\), Newton's second law gives \(mv\frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dt}=P\) on the positive-speed branch.

Integrating gives \(v^2=\frac{450 t}{7} + 36\). The required time is \(\frac{119}{90}\,\mathrm s\).

sections.title: How do I find distance directly under constant power?
sections.label: Pick a position-based equation
sections.intro: If the question gives two speeds and asks for distance, eliminate time using acceleration as a function of position.

blocks.html: With pure drive, \(mv^2\frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dx}=P\).

blocks.title: Use constant power with position as the variable
blocks.prompt: A particle of mass \(5\) kilograms starts with positive speed \(4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). It is driven on a smooth level track by an engine of constant power \(135\,\mathrm W\). Find the distance to reach speed \(7\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

fields.label: Distance to reach the target speed

blocks.hint: When distance is requested, choose the chain-rule acceleration and integrate v squared.
blocks.solution:
Use \(F=\frac Pv\) and \(a=v\frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dx}\). This gives \(mv^2\frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dx}=P\).

Integrating gives \(v^3=81 x + 64\). The requested distance is \(\frac{31}{9}\,\mathrm m\).

blocks.html: Multiplying force by one estimated distance does not model variable drive.

sections.title: How does constant resistance change the limiting speed?
sections.label: Balance the forces at the limit
sections.intro: The forward drive tends to decrease as speed increases. With fixed resistance, the balance speed is approached from a suitable positive-speed initial condition.

blocks.html: Set \(\frac Pv=R\) for the balance speed. At a supplied instant, keep the full resultant when finding acceleration.

blocks.title: Compare constant-power drive and resistance
blocks.prompt: A particle has mass \(5\) kilograms and constant engine power \(135\,\mathrm W\). It moves along a horizontal track against constant resistance \(15\,\mathrm N\). Find its positive limiting speed and signed acceleration at speed \(7\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
blocks.hint: Use the actual known speed for acceleration. Set the net force to zero only to find the steady limit.
blocks.solution:
At positive speed the drive is \(\frac Pv\). Its balance with resistance identifies the limiting speed.

The limiting speed is \(9\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). At the stated smaller speed driving force exceeds resistance.

The acceleration from the force difference divided by mass is \(\frac{6}{7}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

blocks.html: Do not set acceleration to zero at an instant simply because a steady speed exists.

blocks.title: Compare constant-power drive and resistance
blocks.prompt: A particle has mass \(7\) kilograms and constant engine power \(225\,\mathrm W\). It moves along a horizontal track against constant resistance \(\frac{225}{13}\,\mathrm N\). Find its positive limiting speed and signed acceleration at speed \(11\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
blocks.hint: Use the actual known speed for acceleration. Set the net force to zero only to find the steady limit.
blocks.solution:
At positive speed the drive is \(\frac Pv\). Its balance with resistance identifies the limiting speed.

The limiting speed is \(13\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). At the stated smaller speed driving force exceeds resistance.

The acceleration from the force difference divided by mass is \(\frac{450}{1001}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

examples.title: Distinguish an approached boundary from a finite stop
examples.question: A particle starts at the origin. In SI units the speed is \(v=\frac{8}{3} - \frac{2 x}{3}\) while its position is below \(4\). Does it reach \(x=4\) in finite time? Give its limiting coordinate.
solution: Use \(\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}=k(L-x)\) and separate. The initial condition gives \(x=4 - 4 e^{- \frac{2 t}{3}}\).
The exponential is positive at every finite time. Thus the limiting coordinate is \(4\,\mathrm m\) but the particle never arrives there at finite time.

examples.title: Find a finite limiting distance without a finite stop
examples.question: A particle with initial velocity \(6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) coasts with acceleration \(a=- \frac{2 v}{3}\). Find its limiting distance from its starting position and the distance at time \(\frac{3 \log{\left(2 \right)}}{2}\,\mathrm s\).
solution: Separating gives \(v=6 e^{- \frac{2 t}{3}}\). The speed stays positive at all finite times.
Integrating velocity from zero gives \(x=9 - 9 e^{- \frac{2 t}{3}}\).
The limiting distance is \(9\,\mathrm m\). At the stated time it has travelled \(\frac{9}{2}\,\mathrm m\).

examples.title: Use constant power to obtain squared speed in time
examples.question: A particle of mass \(4\) kilograms starts with positive speed \(3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). It is driven on a smooth level track by an engine of constant power \(90\,\mathrm W\). Find the time to reach speed \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
solution: Since \(P=Fv\), Newton's second law gives \(mv\frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dt}=P\) on the positive-speed branch.
Integrating gives \(v^2=45 t + 9\). The required time is \(\frac{16}{45}\,\mathrm s\).

examples.title: Use constant power with position as the variable

Integrating gives \(v^3=\frac{135 x}{2} + 27\). The requested distance is \(\frac{196}{135}\,\mathrm m\).
